blocks.p: Dear Stephen, each one brings something back. Not all of it is anything you’ll want. Take it anyway. It was yours before they took it, and you’re the only one who can carry it now.

The Linnet sailed for Galatia five weeks after the Sedge, on a grey morning with the wind coming up the estuary, and Lyda came down the pier herself with her brother’s kit bag over her shoulder and set it at the foot of the ramp beside Sol’s case. Teo came behind her, with the stitches out of his brow and the splint off his wrist, trying not to look at either of them.

“He’s cleared,” she said. “For crossings. Crew, in a pod, where he can fall down all he likes and nobody’s under him. Never the stick. Lucan wrote never on the form and underlined it twice, and I signed under that.”
Teo looked out at the estuary. He had said very little since Hob Carrow’s door.

“Don’t,” Lyda said, before Sol could speak. “It isn’t for you. He’s asked me for twelve years, and I’ve said no for twelve years, and I was right every time, and I sat in the mud at Reedmouth with his head in my lap and understood what being right had bought him.” She pushed the bag an inch nearer the ramp with her boot. “He’s going. I’d rather it was with my name on the form than yours.”
“Lyda...”

“And the next time there’s a man on a pier,” she said, “you come to me. I’ll say no. Ask anyway.” The wind pulled at her hair. “And the next time he asks you to keep something from me, you tell him you can’t. You’d have got the barge from me the same hour. If you’d told me about the pond, I’d have shouted the roof off, and then I’d have let him. You only had to think I was worth asking.”
“I know that now.”
“Good.” She turned to go, and turned back, and took Lucan’s lenses out of his breast pocket, where he had put them crooked, and put them in straight. “Bring him back the age he left.”
There were no oranges anywhere on Galatia.

That was how Sol knew, afterward, that it had begun before he fell. Below the plateau, where the river had cut down through it, the lowland settlements of Galatia grew grain and little else, strung a day apart along a wide brown river under a high white sky, and the nearest orange was worlds away. But he was standing at the front of the granary at Lowmarch with the grey notebook open in his hands, reading to forty people on benches and grain sacks, and between one line and the next the smell of orange peel came to him so sharp and wet that it might have been torn in front of his face.

He had been reading the psalm about being known. He had chosen it that morning for no reason he could give, except that it had stayed with him through the night. You have searched me, Lord, and you know me. You know when I sit down and when I rise; you understand my thoughts from far away. (Ps. 139:1–2) He held the notebook farther from his eyes than he had in the spring. The lamps hung from the rafters on chains and swayed a little when the wind leaned on the walls, and the dust of a hundred harvests moved in their light.

In the front row a young woman named Rhoda Pask sat with her daughter asleep against her shoulder, three weeks old, a small fierce face in a knitted cap. Her husband Tam sat beside her with his big farmer’s hands folded between his knees. The child’s temples were bare. Sol had noticed it when he came in, the way he had once noticed such things in every cradle he passed, and had looked away.
You hem me in, behind and before, and you lay your hand upon me. (Ps. 139:5)
Teo was on the end of the second bench, mouthing the words. Lucan sat at the back by the door with his cloth-bound book on his knee, writing.
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, and I cannot reach it. (Ps. 139:6)
That was when the oranges came.

He heard himself stop. The smell filled his nose and mouth, and something rose in him from low down, as if a floor had dropped away under his feet, and the lamplight went brighter than lamps could make it, and the granary drew away from him on every side. Somewhere a long way off a man was making a terrible sound, and Sol listened to it with a distant pity and did not know that it was his own.
Then there was rain.

It was hitting a tall window in long diagonal sheets out of a dark sky, running down the glass in threads that caught the light from inside and broke it into a hundred trembling pieces. The light came from long tubes in the ceiling and had a faint hum in it. He could smell the rain through a gap in the old frame, wet stone and something green, and over that solder and burnt coffee and the orange he was peeling.

He was peeling it in one piece. He worked his thumb under the skin and turned the fruit slowly and let the peel come away in a single long spiral that hung down over his wrist, and the oil of it stung a small cut on his knuckle, and he did not mind. His hands were smooth. That was the first thing he knew about himself, before he knew where he was: his hands were smooth and quick and did exactly what he asked of them, and nothing in his back hurt, and he was happy.
He was in a laboratory, long and narrow and cluttered, with benches down both sides covered in instruments and coils of cable and cartons of noodles gone cold, and it was full of people.

They were at the benches all down the long room, working late with the rain on the glass. A broad, round-faced man with a close beard was bent over a schematic, holding it flat against the draft from the window with one big hand; one arm of his spectacles had been mended with black tape. A thin young man with an overbite sat hunched on a stool with a knitted scarf wound twice round his neck, striped green and orange, though the room was warm. Farther down, a tall man had pushed his chair back from the bench and stretched one leg out stiff beneath it, as if the knee would not bend, and was arguing with the ceiling. At the end bench a woman with a long nose turned round with a chipped white mug held in both hands, a cartoon cat on the side of it, and said something to the whole room, and laughed at it herself before she had reached the end, and somebody groaned. Sol knew them all, as a man knows the people he works beside: without thinking about it, without needing to.

At the far end a whiteboard was covered edge to edge in small, slanting, careful handwriting. He knew that hand. He had read it every night for months, by lamplight, on six worlds. Here it was in blue marker, fresh, and the man who had written it was sitting at the bench beside him with his eye to a microscope.
Stephen was young.

He could not have been much past thirty. His hair was dark and too long and stood up at the back where he had slept on it, and his face was unlined and quick and a little sharp, and there was a hole in the elbow of his sweater. He was tapping his foot. He had always tapped his foot. Sol had not known that, and he knew it now, and could not imagine ever having not known it.
“Sol,” Stephen said. “Come here and look at this.”
Sol put the orange down on a paper towel and bent to the second eyepiece.

Under the glass, in a dish of clear gel, lay a sliver no bigger than a fingernail paring: a dark square chip and, around it, fine as a hair, a ring of antenna wire. Stephen touched a key. Current went into the gel, and on the imaging screen beside them the ring lit up, a thin bright circle of false color floating over the chip like a crown.
“Look at that,” Stephen said, delighted. “It’s got a halo.”
“Don’t put that in the paper.”

“Too late. I named the folder. The review board will love it. It sounds holy.” He reached over without asking and took half the orange and pulled it apart. “Tell me again what it’s for. The real version.”

Sol knew the answer as though he had said it in a hundred meetings. “Long-haul crews die out there, and we never know why. The black box tells us what the ship did. It doesn’t tell us what the pilot saw, what she decided and when. This will. It sits at the temple and keeps a running record of the mind, and if the worst happens, we’ll know.” He nodded at the screen. “And your half keeps them alive while they sleep.”

“My half’s the useful half,” Stephen said comfortably. “A pulse in the cold. Keeps the heart honest. Wakes you up at the other end.” He ate a segment. “Your half is the creepy one. It records a man’s soul in case he crashes.”
“It records his decisions. You can have his soul. I don’t need it for the report.”
Stephen laughed. It was a big easy laugh, too loud for the room, and it went through Sol like light through water. He had never heard it. He had heard it a thousand times.
“My mother,” Stephen said, “would tell you there’s only one who’s allowed to read a man that far down.”
“Your mother is welcome to file an objection with the review board.”

“She’d win, too.” But his foot had stopped tapping. He was looking at the bright ring on the screen. “I’m serious, though. Not about God. About people. Anything that can read a mind, somebody is going to want to tidy one. Take the fear out of a pilot before a burn. Take the grief out of a crew after a loss. It’ll sound kind. It’ll sound like medicine.” He looked up. “What happens when somebody decides your recorder ought to talk back?”
Sol had been waiting for the question, he understood, for weeks. He had been looking forward to it. He picked up the fine probe from the bench and bent to the microscope.
“Look,” he said.
At one edge of the chip, where two pathways met, there was a bridge of metal finer than a hair.

“The write path,” Sol said. “You need it at the factory to load the firmware. After that, it’s a door.” He set the tip of the probe against the bridge, steadied his wrist on the bench, and pressed the key. There was a tiny bright spark under the glass and a thread of smoke too small to smell, and the bridge was gone. As he drew the probe back, its heated tip slid off the stage and lay for an instant across the base of his left thumb; he hissed and shook the hand and did not look up, and on the smooth skin a thin line came up white and then red, where he would carry it for four hundred years and never once ask why. “Now it isn’t.”
Stephen let out a breath.

“It reads,” Sol said. “It never writes. Not a machine, not a committee, not a review board with the best intentions in the world. Nothing writes into a human head. If it ever has to, for some reason I can’t imagine, it’ll be a human being who does it, by hand, one person at a time, with a name signed to it.” He laid the probe down. “A human hand on every burn.”
“You and your hands,” Stephen said softly. “And if they build one without the fuse?”
“Then they’ll have to go through me.”
Something went over Stephen’s young face that Sol could not read, fond and rueful and not quite convinced.
“You know what you are?” he said. “You’re the only unbeliever I’ve ever met who’s afraid of playing God.”
“I’m not afraid. I’m careful.”
“In your case,” said Stephen, “that’s the same thing.”
He got up and went to the whiteboard and wrote something at the bottom. Then he held out the marker.
“Sign it. Design release. Your rule, your name. So nobody forgets whose idea it was.”

Sol took the marker. He went to the board, with the orange sharp on his fingers and the rain loud on the glass, and lifted his smooth young hand and set the tip against the white and began to write his name.
The rain went white.
It went white all at once, the way a screen goes white, and the board went white, and Stephen’s face beside him went white and thin and far, and there was nothing in his hand, and he was falling...
“...two minutes, ten,” someone said. “You’re all right. You’re in Lowmarch. Brother Sol. You’re in Lowmarch.”

He was lying on his side on a wooden floor that smelled of grain. Something soft was folded under his head. Every muscle in him was sore, as though he had spent the day hauling grain sacks, and he had bitten his tongue, and above him the lamps were swinging very slightly on their chains. He did not know, for a while, whose the voice was. Then he did. Teo was kneeling beside him, not touching him, with one hand flat on the floor beside his head, exactly as Sol had once knelt beside him on the floor of the dye shed.

There were other faces behind Teo’s. They had not gone anywhere. Some of them were kneeling on the dusty boards, and an old woman at the edge of the light had her eyes shut and her lips moving. No one had covered anyone’s ears.
“Where’s Stephen?” Sol said. It came out slurred. He tried to lift his head to look for him. He had been right there, by the board.
Teo’s face changed.
“Brother Sol,” he said gently. “Stephen’s dead.”

Sol learned it again. He learned it the way you learn a thing in a dream, all at once and with no defense: the market, the cell, the white room under the ice, the needle. He lay on the granary floor with his cheek on someone’s folded coat, and the grief came up through him from somewhere very low, and he did not try to stop it. He wept in front of forty people. Nobody looked away.

They put him to bed in the Pasks’ farmhouse, in a low room under the roof where the wind sang in the eaves. He slept four hours and woke with his head pounding, and found Lucan on a stool by the bed with the book on his knee and a cup of water ready.

“You said three things afterward,” Lucan said, when Sol had drunk. “Before you knew where you were. You said it never writes, four times. You asked for Stephen. And you asked whether anybody had an orange.”

So Sol told him, as exactly as he could, because Lucan would want it exactly: the rain, the noodle cartons, the people at the benches whose faces he had and whose names he did not, the foot tapping, the ring of light. It’s got a halo. Stephen’s pulse and his own recorder. The bridge under the microscope, and the spark, and the probe across his thumb. He turned his left hand over on the blanket while he said it, and looked at the thin shining line he had carried out of that room. When he came to the whiteboard and the marker and his own name, he stopped.
Lucan wrote it all down. The wind leaned on the house.
“The service contact,” he said at last. “Beside the coin. The one I used on Teo.”
“I put it there.” Sol heard his own voice say it, flat and certain, and knew it was true. “So a technician could reach the hardware without opening the skull. I drew it.”
“Then you know what the write path looks like.”
“I burned it. In the first one. With my own hand.”
“And every Halo in every head in the worlds writes,” Lucan said. “Every Renewal. That’s how they take the grief out.”
“Yes.”
“Who put it back?”
“I don’t know,” Sol said.

He did not say the rest. Lucan was a doctor and had sat with a great many people in the hour when they understood something about themselves; he could see it. Sol did not know who had built the next one without the fuse, and the billion after that. He knew only that the man who swore they would have to go through him had lived four hundred years afterward as a bishop of Life, and had held the infants up to the light in the cathedral at Abundance, and sung In the beginning was Life (John 1:1, 4) over their bewildered faces, and laid two fingers on the small soft temples where the coin had just gone in. Whatever had been done had been done through him, or past him, or with his hand on it. He did not know which. He might never know.
“I signed it,” he said. “That’s where it stopped. With my name on the board.”
“A memory isn’t a confession, Tarren,” Lucan said. “It’s evidence. You remember a man who burned a fuse. That’s all you know about him.” He closed the book. “It’s more than I know about most people.”

In the afternoon Tam and Rhoda Pask came up together with the baby. They stood at the foot of the bed, awkward and determined, the way people stand when they have argued all morning and come to the end of it.

“We didn’t want to trouble you today,” Rhoda said. “But the circuit priest comes through in nine days. He does all the new ones at once, at the chapel in Upper Ford.” She shifted the child on her shoulder. “We’ve both gone dark. Since the water. We know what it is now. What it takes.”

“If we don’t let him,” Tam said, “he’ll write her down. An unhaloed child in a Lowmarch family. They’ll ask why. And she’ll never leave Galatia. Never cross. Never see anything but this river.” He looked at his hands. “If we do, it’s in her. Reading her.”
“You were a bishop,” Rhoda said. “You did this. Hundreds of them.”
“Thousands,” Sol said.
“Then tell us what to do.”

She held the child out to him, and he had not meant to take her, and he took her. She was very light and warm through the blanket, and she woke and looked up at him with the grave astonishment of the very new. Under the thin skin at her left temple, where a coin would sit, he could see the faint quick beat of her pulse.

He had built the thing that would go there. He had drawn the seam beside it. He had burned the bridge in the first one and told his friend no one would ever undo it, and he had been wrong, and generations of children had paid for it.
“I don’t know,” he said. “I know what it does. I don’t know what you should do.” He gave her back, carefully, into her mother’s hands. “Give me the time you have. Let me think.”
“Nine days,” Rhoda said.
“I know.”
When they had gone, Teo came up with a lamp and the grey notebook and sat on the stool.
“You stopped in the middle,” he said. “In the granary.” He found the place with his finger. “Can I?”
Sol nodded. Teo read badly, too fast and stumbling on the long words, the way he did everything that required sitting still, and Sol lay and listened with his eyes closed.

“Where can I go from your Spirit? If I go up to the heavens, you are there; if I make my bed in the depths, you are there. If I say, ‘Surely the darkness will hide me,’ even the darkness is not dark to you. The night shines like the day.” (Ps. 139:7–12)
He stopped. He touched his own temple, where the coin was, and Sol saw him think of the word dark and what it meant to them now.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart,” Teo read, more slowly. “Test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” (Ps. 139:23–24)
He closed the notebook.

Search me. Sol had built a thing to search the human heart, and it had searched every heart in the worlds, and kept what it found, and fed on it, and cut out whatever might have turned it around. And here was another searching, older than his, that asked first. That read a man that far down and took nothing. That knew the worst and led him on.
Only one who’s allowed to read a man that far down. Sol had made a joke of it. He would have given anything now to tell Stephen that his mother had been right.
He got up and went down to the Pasks’ kitchen in his stockinged feet. They were still at the table, with the child asleep between them in a drawer lined with fleece.

“Wait,” he said, holding on to the doorframe. “When the priest comes through, take her up into the hills, and hide her if you have to, and let him write down whatever he likes. I don’t know what she’ll lose by it. I know what the coin takes.”
Rhoda looked at Tam. Tam looked at the drawer for a long time.
“There’s a herder’s hut above the Ford,” he said.

When Teo had gone to bed, Sol sat at the little table under the window with paper and a pen. Outside, the wind moved over the grain in long silver waves under the dark, and far off along the river the lights of Upper Ford burned low.
He wrote to Lyda.

He wrote it plainly, as she liked things: the seizure, the laboratory and the rain, Stephen young, the fuse, his name on the board. He wrote that he did not know who had put the door back, and did not know that it was not him. He wrote about the child with the bare temples, and the hut above the Ford.

Then he looked at the hand that held the pen: the knuckles thicker than they had been, a brown spot on the back that had not been there in the spring, a faint tremor when he held it still. It was the same hand. It had peeled the orange and burned the bridge and signed the board. It had signed the custody forms too, thousands of them. Received into Mercy by the hand of Sol Tarren.
He knew why he was writing it to her. Of everyone he loved in all the worlds, she was the only one whose head his hand had never touched.

At the end, before he could think better of it, he wrote: I have asked Lucan whether a man could build one that keeps the heart going in the cold and talks to no one. Stephen’s half, without mine. He says he doesn’t know. He says it the way he says things when he has already started.
